chapters.title: Chapter 2: Covariance, Correlation, and the Mathematics of Diversification

lessons.title: Case Study: Combining Nifty IT and Nifty Bank — Correlation That Actually Diversifies

children.text: Every worked example so far has used individual stocks. Plenty of investors build portfolios out of sector index funds instead, an IT index fund here, a banking index fund there, rather than picking single names. This closing case study for the chapter runs the exact same machinery on Nifty IT and Nifty Bank themselves, and turns up a result that previews the whole of Chapter 3 in miniature.

body.text: Sector indices can diversify each other too, but not always as generously as a hand-picked pair of individual stocks. This case study shows both things at once: real, measurable diversification benefit, and a reminder that correlation, not sector labels, is still the only number that decides how much.

children.text: Why Nifty IT and Nifty Bank

Nifty IT's constituents earn most of their revenue overseas, so they respond to global technology budgets and the rupee-dollar rate. Nifty Bank's constituents earn almost entirely within India, so they respond to RBI repo decisions, credit growth, and domestic asset quality. On paper, this looks like as clean a pairing for diversification as you could ask for.
Twelve Months of Sector Index Returns

body.caption: Monthly returns, Nifty IT and Nifty Bank (illustrative)

children.text: By this point in the course, running mean, standard deviation, covariance, and correlation on a table like this is routine, so here it is done directly in code rather than walked through by hand again.

body.code:
import numpy as np

nifty_it = np.array([6, -5, 9, 2, -9, 5, 10, -4, 7, -8, 3, -2])
nifty_bank = np.array([3, 5, 6, 6, -7, 3, 7, -2, 2, -9, -5, 6])

for name, series in [("Nifty IT", nifty_it), ("Nifty Bank", nifty_bank)]:
    m, s = series.mean(), series.std()
    print(f"{name}: mean {m:.2f}% monthly ({m*12:.1f}% annualized), "
          f"std {s:.2f}% monthly ({s*np.sqrt(12):.2f}% annualized)")

covariance = np.cov(nifty_it, nifty_bank, ddof=0)[0, 1]
correlation = np.corrcoef(nifty_it, nifty_bank)[0, 1]
print(f"Covariance: {covariance:.2f}")
print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.2f}")
body.caption: Same formulas as every earlier lesson, just run in one pass instead of by hand.

body.text: 0.63 is noticeably higher than the 0.32 correlation Chapter 1 found between individual stocks TCS and Maruti Suzuki. This is not a coincidence. Each sector index has already averaged away its own constituents' company-specific noise: a bad quarter at one bank gets diluted by eleven other banks in the index. What is left over in each index is weighted more heavily toward the shared, market-wide component, and market-wide moves tend to hit every sector at once. Picking individual stocks across genuinely different sectors, as Chapter 1 did, is generally a more powerful diversification lever than picking sector indices against each other.

children.text: Portfolio Risk Across the Full Weight Range
With variance and covariance in hand, Lesson 2's formula prices every possible weight combination instantly, no combined return series required at any point.

body.caption: Annualized portfolio volatility by weight in Nifty IT

body.title: Portfolio volatility as the Nifty IT weight changes

body.text: Look at where the curve bottoms out. It is not at either pure extreme. 100% Nifty Bank sits at 18.55%, and 100% Nifty IT sits at 21.86%, but the lowest point on the entire curve, around 28-30% Nifty IT and 70-72% Nifty Bank, comes in at roughly 17.87%, BELOW both pure single-index portfolios. This is precisely Chapter 1's TCS-and-Maruti-Suzuki surprise, showing up again at the index level, and it is no longer something you have to build a whole case study to find. It fell straight out of a table of formula results.

children.text: This lesson found that minimum by scanning across eleven weight combinations and reading off the lowest one. That works for two assets and a handful of weights. Chapter 3 gives you the actual formula that solves for this minimum-variance weight directly, for any number of assets, without scanning anything.
Turning This Into a Real Portfolio

A two-fund sector tilt like this is genuinely implementable on NSE, through Nifty IT and Nifty Bank index funds or ETFs offered by several Indian AMCs, without needing to pick individual stocks within either sector at all. Two practical points carry over directly from earlier lessons. First, from Lesson 3 of Chapter 1: weights drift on their own as prices move, so a 30/70 split built today will not stay 30/70, and needs periodic rebalancing to keep the risk profile this lesson calculated. Second, from Lesson 1 of this chapter: 0.63 is a normal-times correlation, and it should be expected to climb during a broad market selloff, when both sectors get pulled down by the same risk-off flows.

body.title: Price a weight combination not in the table
body.prompt: Using this lesson's numbers, Var(Nifty IT) = 39.81, Var(Nifty Bank) = 28.69, Cov(IT, Bank) = 21.38, all monthly and in percent-squared, what is the ANNUALIZED portfolio volatility for a 65% Nifty IT / 35% Nifty Bank split?
body.explanation: Monthly variance = (0.65)^2(39.81) + (0.35)^2(28.69) + 2(0.65)(0.35)(21.38) = 16.82 + 3.51 + 9.73 = 30.06. Monthly standard deviation = the square root of 30.06, about 5.48%. Annualized: 5.48 x the square root of 12 is approximately 19.0%.

body.title: Why the minimum isn't at either end
body.question: In this lesson's table, why does portfolio risk bottom out around 30% Nifty IT / 70% Nifty Bank, rather than at 0% or 100% in either index?
options: Because Nifty Bank is always the safer choice, so more of it is always better

Because the two indices are not perfectly correlated (0.63, not 1), so blending them lets some of their swings offset each other, up to a point where adding more of the higher-volatility index starts outweighing that benefit
Because the table contains a calculation error and the true minimum is at 0% Nifty IT
Because portfolio risk is always minimized at a 50/50 split for any two assets
body.explanation: With correlation below 1, blending the two indices offsets some of their independent swings, pulling risk below Nifty Bank's own 18.55%. But Nifty IT is also the more volatile of the two individually, so past a certain point, adding more of it starts raising risk faster than the diversification benefit can offset. The minimum sits where these two effects balance, which is neither extreme and not automatically the midpoint either.

body.title: Sector funds versus individual stocks
body.scenario: An investor is deciding between two diversification approaches: (A) a two-fund portfolio of Nifty IT and Nifty Bank index funds, like this lesson's case study, or (B) Chapter 1's approach of hand-picking individual stocks across different sectors, like TCS and Maruti Suzuki.
body.prompt: Based on the correlation numbers from this chapter, which approach is likely to deliver a larger diversification benefit, and why might an investor still choose the other one anyway?
body.modelAnswer: Approach B, hand-picked individual stocks across sectors, showed a lower correlation (0.32) than approach A's sector indices (0.63), so it is likely to deliver a larger diversification benefit for the same number of holdings. An investor might still choose sector index funds anyway for practical reasons this chapter has not covered: lower research and monitoring effort, no single-company risk from a bad stock pick within a sector, lower transaction costs from holding two funds instead of many individual stocks, and easier rebalancing. Diversification benefit is one input into that decision, not the only one.

cards.definition: The average product of two assets' deviations from their own means. Positive if they tend to move together, negative if apart.
Covariance rescaled by both standard deviations, always between -1 and +1, and comparable across any pair of assets.
w1^2 sigma1^2 + w2^2 sigma2^2 + 2 w1 w2 Cov12. The cross term is the only place diversification benefit comes from.
The matrix form of portfolio variance for any number of assets, using the full covariance matrix and the weight vector.
Correlation between diversified indices, which tends to run higher than correlation between individual stocks, since each index has already averaged away its own constituents' company-specific noise.

points: Nifty IT and Nifty Bank showed a correlation of 0.63, positive and real diversification benefit exists, but meaningfully higher than the 0.32 correlation Chapter 1 found between individual stocks TCS and Maruti Suzuki.

Sector indices tend to correlate with each other more than individual stocks do, because each index has already diversified away its own constituents' company-specific noise, leaving relatively more shared market-wide risk exposed.
Scanning portfolio risk across the full weight range, from 0% to 100% Nifty IT, produced a curve that bottoms out around 30% Nifty IT / 70% Nifty Bank, below the risk of holding either index alone.
This minimum-risk point is neither a pure single-asset holding nor an automatic 50/50 split. Its exact location depends on both assets' variances and their covariance together.

This chapter's full toolkit, covariance, correlation, the two-asset variance formula, and the covariance matrix, now lets you price any portfolio's risk directly from a handful of estimated numbers, without ever constructing a combined return series.

Chapter 3 formalizes what this lesson found by scanning a table: a direct formula for the minimum-variance weight, and the full efficient frontier of every optimal risk-return combination available from a set of assets.
